flagged.evidence: Rule details page: goto_next "Stops evaluating other rules in the firewall policy, and evaluates rules in the next step of the firewall policy and rule evaluation order." The fact is correct, but the statement gives its own answer away: the action name goto_next literally says 'go to next', so a player who knows nothing about Cloud NGFW can guess True from the words 'delegates ... to later policy evaluation with goto_next'. That breaks the prompt's 'no name giveaway' and 'no wording tells' rules. The more decisive design fact here is that a matching allow or deny in a hierarchical policy ends all evaluation. https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order says: Allow: "the rule allows the traffic, and all rule evaluation stops"; Goto_next: "the rule evaluation continues to ... A hierarchical firewall policy associated with a folder ancestor closer to the target resource, if it exists."
flagged.problem: Name giveaway: the meaning of goto_next is readable from the keyword, so the card tests reading, not knowledge. The subject is also slightly off, since a rule in the policy carries the action, not the policy itself.

Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order (Policy and rule evaluation order). verdicts.notes:
I checked all 10 section 2.2 cards (5 true, 5 false), all in raw/gcp-pca-b2.json. Every source URL loaded on 2026-10-08, is an official docs.cloud.google.com page and supports its card. Evidence for the eight cards that pass:
- s2.2-01, Autoclass: "When an object's data is read, the object transitions to Standard storage if it's not already stored in Standard storage." Reading only metadata does not trigger the move, and the card says "reads it", so it holds.
- s2.2-03, soft delete: "preserves objects and buckets that get deleted or overwritten". Restoring "creates a new, live copy of that object within the same bucket". The statement says "can", which covers buckets with Object Versioning on, where an overwritten object becomes noncurrent first.
- s2.2-04, Local SSD: "Local SSD storage is not automatically replicated and all data on the Local SSD may be lost..."
- s2.2-05, snapshots: "For unchanged data, snapshots reference the data in previous snapshots", and "a snapshot might occasionally capture a full image of the disk". The explanation covers that caveat.
- s2.2-06, Cloud SQL HA: "The standby instance cannot be used for read queries." The only exception the page names is the legacy MySQL HA configuration, which is no longer offered.
- s2.2-07, Spanner editions: the page lists dual-region and multi-region configurations only under Enterprise Plus. Small wording point: an instance has the configuration, not a database. Not flagged.
- s2.2-08, Bigtable: multi-cluster routing "provides eventual consistency". Read-your-writes is possible only with single-cluster routing, and even row-affinity routing does not guarantee it. Small wording point: "by default" in the statement adds nothing. Not flagged.
- s2.2-09, BigQuery replication: "The primary replica is writable, and the secondary replica is read-only."

No duplicates within the deck:

duplicates.why: Both rest on the same Google position: accept a planned cutover outage rather than chase zero downtime. 1.4-05 says Google advises against needless zero-downtime requirements. 5.1-05 says Google stops source writes before promoting a DMS job, which is a planned write outage. Knowing either answer gives the other. 1.4-05 is also a self-refuting strawman, because the statement itself says the workloads 'tolerate planned cutover outages'.

conflictGroups.name: regional-zone-only-failover
conflictGroups.why: The explanations of 1.2-03 ('a regional deployment uses zones within one region') and 2.3-05 ('replicas in different zones of one region') hand the player the rule that regional HA stays inside one region. That gives away 1.2-05 (Cloud SQL HA standby in another region, false). 1.2-05's explanation ('different zones of the same region ... protects against a zonal failure') in turn gives away 1.2-03 (automatic failover to another region, false).

conflictGroups.name: cloud-sql-ha-standby
conflictGroups.why: Both test the Cloud SQL HA standby. 2.2-06's explanation ('the standby reserves its role for failover') and 1.2-05's explanation (standby placed for zonal failover protection) each describe the standby purely as a failover target, which hints at the other card's answer.

conflictGroups.name: migration-cutover-downtime
conflictGroups.why: 5.1-05's explanation (stop source writes before promotion) shows that Google accepts a planned cutover outage, which gives away 1.4-05 (Google recommends zero downtime, false). The reverse also holds. This is the duplicate pair; keep them apart if both stay.

conflictGroups.name: guardrail-beyond-iam
conflictGroups.why: 3.1-02 (org policy blocks key creation 'even when IAM permits', true) and 3.1-06 (VPC SC restricts 'despite permissive IAM grants', true) form a mirrored pair with the same structure: a second control that overrides IAM. Seeing one primes True for the other. 2.4-09's explanation ('Granting Google Cloud IAM access leaves those source permissions in force') teaches the same lesson, that IAM is not the final word, and so reinforces the pair.

conflictGroups.name: non-retroactive-effect
conflictGroups.why: All four rest on one principle: a new policy, label, sink or TTL affects only later events. The explanation of each one states that principle: 3.2-08 says the location constraint 'applies to new resource creation'; 6.1-04 says the sink leaves 'earlier stored entries' alone rather than replaying them; 4.2-06 says 'earlier usage retains its earlier attribution'; 1.4-10 says the lower TTL waits for 'the previous cached value'. Any one of them predicts the answers of the others.

conflictGroups.name: cloud-deploy-rollout-per-target
conflictGroups.why: 4.1-03's explanation ('Promoting a release creates a rollout for its destination target') and 4.1-04's explanation ('approvals authorize a rollout to a specific target') teach that every Cloud Deploy action is its own rollout bound to one target. That gives away 6.3-05 (rollback creates a new rollout, true) and lets each of the 4.1 cards answer the other.

conflictGroups.name: cloud-run-traffic-allocation
conflictGroups.why: 6.3-04's explanation ('a team changes the traffic allocation explicitly to return traffic') describes the routing-based rollback that 6.3-02 tests. 6.3-02's explanation ('restores an existing revision by changing traffic allocation') in turn suggests that traffic stays where the team routed it, which hints that 6.3-04 is false.

conflictGroups.name: realistic-testing-conditions
conflictGroups.why: All four reward one heuristic: Google wants tests under production-like conditions. 6.3-08's statement and explanation ('adds realistic request load to simulated outages ... while users are active') nearly give away 6.3-10 (isolated Spanner load test, false). 5.1-09 (production-like pre-production, true) and 4.1-09's explanation ('testing the application stack ... with restored data') point the same way.

conflictGroups.name: bigtable-weak-guarantees
conflictGroups.why: 2.2-08's explanation (multi-cluster routing 'offers eventual consistency') and 1.3-06's explanation ('atomic transaction boundary is a single row') both describe Bigtable's limited guarantees. Each strongly hints that the other card's stronger-guarantee statement is false.

conflictGroups.name: adc-credential-sources
conflictGroups.why: Both test Application Default Credentials sources. 5.2-02's explanation ('a file left in the environment can change which identity a deployed workload uses') hints that production should rely on the attached service account (5.2-01, true). 5.2-01's explanation ('obtains credentials from its environment rather than carrying a key file') muddies 5.2-02's precedence question when both cards come up in one round.

The average length of true and false statements is within 5 characters in every section (largest gaps: 2.4, where false statements are 4.6 characters longer; 2.1, where true statements are 4.0 longer; 1.2, where false statements are 3.6 longer; overall 101.8 vs 101.0). No statement is over 120 characters, and none contains a banned negation or absolute. The tells are in wording and templates, not length.

1) Who the statement cites. 'The Well-Architected Framework ...': 7 true, 0 false (s1.2-01, s1.2-02, s1.4-09, s4.2-01, s4.2-09, s4.2-10, s6.1-01). Answering True on any framework card scores 100%. 'recommends' overall: 13 true, 4 false. 'Google recommends': 8 true (s1.1-04, s1.2-04, s1.4-08, s4.1-08, s4.1-10, s5.1-09, s5.2-01, s6.3-08) and 4 false (s1.4-05, s4.1-09, s5.1-05, s6.3-10). All 4 false recommendations endorse a weaker or riskier practice: zero downtime for workloads that tolerate outages, file checks instead of stack tests, writes during promotion, an isolated load test. So the rule 'a Google recommendation is true unless it sounds lax' scores 17 out of 17. s1.4-05 and s4.1-09 are strawmen: nobody who studied believes Google recommends less testing, or zero downtime for outage-tolerant workloads.

2) Loophole or relaxation template, false 12 times: s1.4-10 shortens cache entries, s2.2-02 shortens a locked retention policy, s2.4-09 overrides ACLs, s3.1-01 reduces inherited permissions, s3.1-05 replaces a version payload, s3.2-08 suspends existing resources, s3.2-09 transfers compliance evaluation, s4.1-04 carries an approval forward, s4.2-07 pauses commitment fees, s6.3-03 exempts VMs from quotas, s6.3-04 resets the traffic split, s6.1-10 retains elapsed time. Only about 2 true cards have this shape (s3.1-04 EKM revokes access, s2.3-03 retains a Spot VM). The prompt allows at most two false cards per template.

3) Boundary-crossing template ('X extends to another region, network or scope'), false 7 times: s1.1-05, s1.2-03, s1.2-05, s2.1-06, s2.1-09, s4.1-01, s5.2-10. True 3 times: s1.2-06, s2.3-08, s6.1-09.

4) Scope-narrowing verbs 'limits' and 'confines': 0 true, 4 false (s2.3-04, s2.3-06, s3.1-08, s6.1-06). All four use the template 'X limits Y to a single Z'.

5) 'preserves' as the main verb: 0 true, 4 false (s1.2-10, s1.3-03, s5.1-08, s5.2-06). The wider preserve, retain and keep family: 4 true (s2.3-03, s2.3-05, s5.1-07, s5.2-08) and 9 false (s1.1-03, s1.2-10, s1.3-03, s2.2-04, s2.3-09, s4.1-02, s5.1-08, s5.2-06, s6.1-10).

6) 'automatically' is balanced overall (9 true, 8 false), but 'automatically' plus a protective action is a false template 4 times: s1.2-03 fails over, s2.1-08 blocks, s2.2-04 replicates, s3.2-07 blocks deletion. True uses of 'automatically' describe mechanisms instead (s2.3-01, s2.2-01, s3.2-05, s6.3-05, s6.3-06).

7) Hedge verbs are lopsided. 'lets': 4 true (s1.1-08, s1.3-01, s1.3-04, s2.1-05), 8 false (s1.3-02, s1.4-07, s2.1-06, s2.1-10, s2.2-02, s2.3-09, s3.2-02, s6.1-05). 'allows': 0 true, 2 false (s3.1-01, s6.1-02). 'can' is roughly balanced (21 true, 16 false), and 'supports' is balanced (3 and 3), but 'supports X for applications that need Y' is false twice (s1.3-06, s1.3-08) against 1 true (s1.3-05).

8) Small markers. 'while': 7 true (s1.1-09, s1.3-01, s1.3-09, s2.1-03, s3.2-03, s5.1-01, s6.1-03), 3 false (s2.2-06, s5.1-05, s6.1-02). 'even when' or 'despite': 2 true, 0 false (s3.1-02, s3.1-06). 'same': 2 true, 0 false (s1.1-08, s4.1-03). 'also': 0 true, 2 false (s1.1-01, s2.1-09). 'own': 0 true, 2 false (s2.2-09, s6.3-09). 'by default': 4 true, 6 false (false: s1.3-10, s2.2-08, s2.3-04, s2.3-09, s2.4-02, s6.3-04). 'requires': 2 true, 3 false, which is fine.

9) The subject predicts the answer. Statements starting with 'Cloud Run': 1 true, 4 false (s1.2-10, s1.3-08, s2.3-07, s6.3-04). Starting with 'Cloud Deploy': 4 true, 1 false (s4.1-04).

10) Difficulty, if the game ever shows it: difficulty 3 is 8 true and 24 false (75% false); difficulty 1 is 37 true and 27 false.

11) Truism-like cards that a player answers from common sense: s1.1-02 (tighter recovery targets cost more), s1.1-01 (meeting the RPO also meets the RTO), s1.1-07 (lower CPU use cuts the bill of an unchanged VM), s3.2-09 (a BAA transfers compliance evaluation to Google), s6.3-09 (pen testing your own projects requires notification).

source.title: Combine reservations with committed use discounts

rewrite.reason: weak_card (definition card); verifier's cold-pattern replacement, confirmed by the planning guide's flat-tire analogy (Cold: no spare tire, trip stops until help arrives)
rewrite.statement: Google's DR guide describes the cold pattern as one with spare recovery resources already in place before a disaster.
rewrite.explanation: In the cold pattern no spare resources are on hand, so recovery must first obtain them, and the service stays down until they arrive.
rewrite.misconception: The cold DR pattern keeps spare recovery resources provisioned before a disaster.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (metric name gives the answer); verifier's replacement, confirmed on dora.dev: 'DORA uses three factors to measure software delivery throughput: Change lead time, Deployment frequency, Failed deployment recovery time'. Set volatility may_change (DORA regrouped its metrics recently).
rewrite.statement: DORA groups failed deployment recovery time with deployment frequency as a software delivery throughput factor.
rewrite.explanation: DORA measures throughput with change lead time, deployment frequency and failed deployment recovery time; change fail rate and deployment rework rate measure instability.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the cited CUD overview has no capacity sentence. The new page says compute flexible commitments 'don't require or support attached reservations' and 'don't come with assured capacity'. Statement and answer are unchanged; the explanation is tightened to match the page.
rewrite.statement: Compute flexible committed use discounts can reserve VM capacity for the committed workload.
rewrite.explanation: Compute flexible commitments don't support attached reservations and come with no assured capacity, so a workload that needs assured VM capacity uses a separate reservation.
rewrite.misconception: Purchasing a compute flexible commitment also secures the workload's VM capacity.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Combine reservations with committed use discounts

rewrite.reason: weak_card (generic HA truism); verifier's sizing-rule replacement, confirmed: 'Google recommends overprovisioning your group by at least 50%' (three or more zones) and 'doubling' for two zones. Set volatility may_change because it uses a number.
rewrite.statement: For a regional MIG spread across three zones, Google recommends overprovisioning the group by at least 50%.
rewrite.explanation: Losing one of three zones removes a third of capacity, so Google recommends at least 50% extra instances, and doubling for two zones, so the remaining zones carry the full load.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (textbook identification); verifier's tier-constraint replacement, confirmed: 'Cloud CDN is always Premium Tier. You cannot use Standard Tier with Cloud CDN.' It also puts 'requires' in a true statement.
rewrite.statement: Enabling Cloud CDN caching on a load balancer requires that load balancer to use Network Service Tiers' Premium Tier.
rewrite.explanation: Cloud CDN is always Premium Tier and can't be used with Standard Tier, so choosing Standard Tier to lower a load balancer's egress cost rules out Cloud CDN caching.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous (project deletion could remove backups); now limited to manual deletion, as the page states: 'backups are completely immutable—they cannot be manually deleted by you, any other user, or Google until your specified duration has passed'. The automatic lien starting 2026-11-01 is left out.
rewrite.statement: A Project Owner can manually delete a backup vault's backups before their enforced retention ends.
rewrite.explanation: Enforced retention makes a vault's backups immutable: no user, including a Project Owner, and not even Google can manually delete them until the retention period has passed.
rewrite.misconception: Project Owner permissions override a backup vault's enforced retention.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Backup vaults for immutable and indelible backups

rewrite.reason: weak_card (restates Shared VPC's purpose); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'each service project can only be attached to a single host project'. Lengthened to keep 1.3's true and false lengths balanced.
rewrite.statement: Each Shared VPC service project attaches to a single host project, though one host can serve many service projects.
rewrite.explanation: A host project shares subnets with many service projects, but each service project can be attached to only one host project, so it uses that one host's Shared VPC network.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous (the PROXY protocol lets a proxy NLB preserve the client IP); now about the default, confirmed: 'By default, the target proxy does not preserve the original client IP address and port information. You can preserve this information by enabling the PROXY protocol'
rewrite.statement: By default, an external proxy Network Load Balancer passes client source IPs and ports through to its backends.
rewrite.explanation: By default the target proxy drops the original client IP and port, so backends see the proxy as the source. Enabling the PROXY protocol on the target proxy preserves that client information.
rewrite.misconception: A proxy Network Load Balancer hands each client's source IP to backends with no extra configuration.
rewrite.sourceTitle: External proxy Network Load Balancer overview

rewrite.reason: weak_card (truism); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'expand each group to assign up to four preference sets that you want to compare'. The number is left out.
rewrite.statement: One Migration Center TCO report can compare several migration preference sets for one asset group.
rewrite.explanation: When generating a TCO report, a team picks asset groups and assigns each group multiple preference sets, so one report compares migration scenarios side by side.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (strawman); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'after a rehost migration, the workloads that are running in the target environment aren't optimized for the cloud'
rewrite.statement: Rehosted workloads run optimized for the cloud once they reach the Google Cloud target environment.
rewrite.explanation: Rehost moves workloads with minor or no changes, so Google notes they aren't optimized for the cloud afterwards and miss features such as horizontal scalability; replatform or refactor work adds that.
rewrite.misconception: A lift-and-shift migration leaves workloads optimized for the cloud.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started

rewrite.reason: weak_card (near-copy definition, 'purchased' gives away 'repurchase'); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'you can move from on-premises collaboration software and local storage to Google Workspace'
rewrite.statement: Google classifies replacing on-premises collaboration software with Google Workspace as a repurchase migration.
rewrite.explanation: Repurchase means moving from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted SaaS equivalent, rather than moving its code or rebuilding it.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started

rewrite.reason: weak_card (definition of clustering); verifier's replacement. The page says 'you don't receive an accurate query cost estimate before query execution' and BigQuery 'attempts to reduce the total bytes at execution'. The page does not use the words 'upper bound', so the statement says 'can exceed'.
rewrite.statement: BigQuery's pre-run cost estimate for a query on a clustered table can exceed the bytes the query finally scans.
rewrite.explanation: BigQuery learns which clustered blocks it can skip only during execution, so the estimate before a run isn't exact and the final cost reflects the blocks scanned. Partitioning gives granular pre-run estimates.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (answer readable from stop versus delete); verifier's in-scope replacement, confirmed: 'Spot VMs don't have a minimum or maximum runtime unless you specifically limit the runtime'. Reworded to avoid negation.
rewrite.statement: A Spot VM keeps running until Compute Engine preempts it unless the team sets a limit on its run duration.
rewrite.explanation: Spot VMs have no minimum or maximum runtime unless you limit it, so a long batch job keeps running until preemption or until a run duration limit the team configured ends it.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous ('Autopilot mode' could be read as the cluster mode); now names the managed nodes. Confirmed: 'You control the cluster and can run your own Standard node pools alongside the nodes that GKE manages.'
rewrite.statement: Workloads a GKE Standard cluster puts on Autopilot-managed nodes run in a separate Autopilot cluster.
rewrite.explanation: Autopilot ComputeClasses let a Standard cluster run selected workloads on Autopilot-managed node pools alongside the team's own Standard node pools, in the same cluster.
rewrite.misconception: Autopilot-managed workloads need their own Autopilot cluster when a team also runs Standard node pools.
rewrite.sourceTitle: About Autopilot mode workloads in GKE Standard

rewrite.reason: explanation_error (taught the removed Elevate privilege feature). Confirmed on the how-to page: 'the integration does not provide the Elevate privilege feature. To perform these tasks, you can use a solution user account to: Configure identity sources...'. The 'permanently' wording is removed.
rewrite.statement: VMware Engine gives the default vCenter user full administrator access to vCenter in a private cloud.
rewrite.explanation: The default vCenter user has privileges for normal day-to-day operations. Administrative tasks such as configuring identity sources use the solution user accounts that VMware Engine creates.
rewrite.misconception: The default vCenter user holds full vCenter administrator rights.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (truism with hedge); verifier's in-scope replacement, confirmed: 'For a managed Slurm experience, you can use Cluster Director. To use Slurm natively, you can use Cluster Toolkit (which offers cluster blueprints that automatically install Slurm...)'. The Cluster Director overview has no Preview label.
rewrite.statement: Cluster Director gives AI Hypercomputer GPU clusters a managed Slurm environment, so teams skip installing Slurm.
rewrite.explanation: For a managed Slurm experience Google points to Cluster Director, while Cluster Toolkit deploys blueprints that install Slurm on clusters the team runs itself.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Plan and create your AI infrastructure

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the cited IAM page does not cover source ACLs. The new page says 'Google uses your identity provider to identify the end user performing a search and determine if they have access to the documents' and 'never bypasses source system access controls or grants additional permissions'. Statement and answer are unchanged; the explanation is tightened.
rewrite.statement: Gemini Enterprise uses project IAM grants to override source-document ACLs for ACL-enabled connectors.
rewrite.explanation: Gemini Enterprise uses your identity provider to check whether the end user can access each document a connector returns; IAM roles on the project grant no extra document access.
rewrite.misconception: Project IAM roles replace source-document permissions when a third-party connector enforces ACLs.

rewrite.reason: duplicate of gcp-ace-s4.1-04; replaced with the verifier's uncovered 3.1 scope fact. Confirmed: 'Cloud KMS doesn't let you destroy key versions immediately', 'The default scheduled for destruction duration is 30 days', restore is possible during that period. Set volatility may_change (30-day figure).
rewrite.statement: Cloud KMS destroys a key version's material as soon as an administrator schedules that version for destruction.
rewrite.explanation: A key version waits in the scheduled-for-destruction state, 30 days by default and configurable at key creation, and can be restored during that time.
rewrite.misconception: Scheduling a key version for destruction destroys its key material immediately.

rewrite.reason: duplicate of gcp-ace-s4.2-07; replaced with the verifier's context-aware access fact. Confirmed: IAP access policies extend with access levels that 'allow access restrictions to resources based on IP address and end-user device attributes'; 'IAP uses the access level name to associate it with a IAP-secured app'; device attributes need a Chrome Enterprise Premium license.
rewrite.statement: Identity-Aware Proxy can apply Access Context Manager access levels, such as device or IP conditions, to app users.
rewrite.explanation: IAP attaches access levels to the IAM grants of an IAP-secured app, so users get in only from approved IP ranges or trusted devices; device attributes need a Chrome Enterprise Premium license.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Setting up context-aware access with Identity-Aware Proxy

rewrite.reason: weak_card (name giveaway, near-copy); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'set a policy on Cloud KMS keys to view, approve, and deny key access requests depending on the provided justification code', available for select control packages. Set volatility may_change.
rewrite.statement: Key Access Justifications lets a key policy deny a Cloud KMS request by its justification code.
rewrite.explanation: Beyond logging why a key is used, Key Access Justifications policies can approve or deny key access per justification code; this depends on the Assured Workloads control package chosen.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (definition of preview); verifier's replacement, reworded to avoid negation. Confirmed: 'Before you create a new deployment or update a deployment, you can preview the deployment' and 'A preview executes the Terraform plan command'.
rewrite.statement: Infrastructure Manager can preview a new deployment before the team creates any of its resources.
rewrite.explanation: An Infrastructure Manager preview runs Terraform plan for a new deployment or an update, so the team reviews the resources planned for provisioning before anything is created.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (near-copy of the source sentence, common-sense blameless idea); verifier's trigger replacement, confirmed: 'Interventions from on-call engineers, such as a release rollback or rerouting of traffic.' Worded as 'Google lists' rather than 'Google recommends' to ease that tell.
rewrite.statement: Google lists an on-call intervention, such as a release rollback, among the triggers for a postmortem.
rewrite.explanation: Google's postmortem criteria include on-call interventions such as a release rollback or rerouted traffic, alongside user-visible downtime, data loss of any kind and monitoring failures.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (strawman 'in place of'); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'To test backups, restore them in a non-production environment' and 'a data restoration test must include testing of the entire application stack and all the critical infrastructure services with the restored data'
rewrite.statement: Google recommends restoring backups into the production environment when testing that they are usable.
rewrite.explanation: Google recommends restoring backups in a non-production environment and testing the entire application stack and critical infrastructure services with the restored data.
rewrite.misconception: Restoring backups into production is the recommended way to prove they are usable.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Perform testing for recovery from data loss

rewrite.reason: weak_card (near-copy truism); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'Make sure that you grant users the same access to the DR environment that they have in the source production environment' and the IaC note on replicating IAM policies. Reworded without 'same', which was a true-only word.
rewrite.statement: Google recommends granting users in the DR environment the access they hold in production.
rewrite.explanation: Users must be able to work in the recovered environment; when production runs on Google Cloud, IaC tools such as Terraform can replicate its IAM policies in the DR environment.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (the statement did not test non-retroactivity); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'The cost data for a specific label only shows usage from the date that the label was applied to a resource.'
rewrite.statement: Cloud Billing exports show a new label's costs only from the date the label was applied to a resource.
rewrite.explanation: Labels aren't retroactive: the export shows a label's costs from the date it was applied, so apply labels before the period you need to allocate.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (definition of 'commitment'); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'you are still responsible for the full cost of the commitment. No rollover: Unused commitment does not carry over to the next hour.'
rewrite.statement: Unused spend-based commitment in one hour carries over to cover eligible usage above the commitment in a later hour.
rewrite.explanation: Spend-based commitments apply hourly: when eligible usage in an hour falls below the commitment you still pay the full amount, and the unused part doesn't roll over.
rewrite.misconception: Unused spend-based commitment banks credit for later hours.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (invented 'submitted forecasts' feature); verifier's replacement, confirmed: recommendations use 'a formula that analyzes historical and recent usage metrics gathered by Cloud Billing, and includes usage covered by existing commitments'. Scenario modeling only adjusts the term, coverage and history window, not forecasts.
rewrite.statement: Cloud Billing sizes its CUD recommendations from an organization's expected future usage growth.
rewrite.explanation: CUD recommendations come from historical and recent usage, including usage already covered by commitments, so architects weigh planned growth or decline themselves.
rewrite.misconception: CUD recommendations are sized from forecast business growth.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Get recommendations for committed use discounts (CUDs)

rewrite.reason: weak_card (generic management truism, really a 6.1 principle); verifier's replacement. The page (Standard) gives activation steps for new and existing clusters, adds k8s-namespace and workload labels to the detailed export, and says costs show no GKE labels 'when GKE cost allocation is not enabled'. The verifier's quote 'not enabled by default' was not found on the page, so the card rests on the activation requirement. Set volatility may_change.
rewrite.statement: GKE cost allocation must be enabled on a Standard cluster before billing exports show its namespace costs.
rewrite.explanation: Once GKE cost allocation is enabled, the detailed Cloud Billing export to BigQuery carries cluster, namespace and workload labels for chargeback; otherwise those costs carry no GKE labels.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Get key spending insights for your GKE resource allocation and cluster costs

rewrite.reason: out_of_scope (iterator paging is developer depth); verifier's in-scope emulator replacement, confirmed: 'The emulator doesn't support the following: TLS/HTTPS, authentication, Identity and Access Management (IAM), permissions, or roles.'
rewrite.statement: The Spanner emulator enforces IAM permissions on requests that an application's integration tests send to it.
rewrite.explanation: The Spanner emulator supports no authentication, IAM, permissions or roles, so access grants still need testing against a real Spanner instance.
rewrite.misconception: The Spanner emulator reproduces production IAM enforcement for tests.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: moved to the state-file page ('the Terraform state file that is created for each deployment and revision'). Statement tightened as the verifier suggested; same fact and answer.
rewrite.statement: Infrastructure Manager keeps a Terraform state file per deployment and per revision.
rewrite.explanation: Infrastructure Manager creates a Terraform state file per deployment and per revision; a team can download a state file to inspect or modify it.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (the statement did not test the fact); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'Log sinks can't retroactively route log entries' and 'you can retroactively copy log data from a log bucket to Cloud Storage'
rewrite.statement: To export logs received before a sink existed, Cloud Logging offers a copy from the log bucket to Cloud Storage.
rewrite.explanation: Sinks route only entries that arrive after they're created; for entries already stored in a log bucket, Cloud Logging can copy them retroactively to Cloud Storage.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (product identification); verifier's replacement, confirmed: the supported-environments table marks 'Outside of Google Cloud' Y for Go, Java, Node.js and Python
rewrite.statement: Cloud Profiler can collect profiles from applications that run outside Google Cloud, such as on premises.
rewrite.explanation: Cloud Profiler agents for Go, Java, Node.js and Python also run outside Google Cloud, so hybrid workloads can send low-overhead CPU and heap profiles to a Google Cloud project.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (strawman quota exemption); verifier's replacement, confirmed: with maxUnavailable 0 and maxSurge above 0 'Compute Engine removes each old machine only after its replacement new machine is created and running', and 'maxSurge only works if you have enough quota or resources'
rewrite.statement: Setting maxUnavailable to 0 in a MIG rolling update removes the need for spare quota during the update.
rewrite.explanation: With maxUnavailable at 0 and maxSurge above 0, the MIG creates each replacement VM before deleting the old one, and maxSurge only works when there is quota and capacity for the extra VMs.
rewrite.misconception: A rolling update with zero unavailable VMs needs no extra quota.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Automatically apply VM configuration updates in a MIG

rewrite.reason: weak_card (near-copy of the source sentence); verifier's replacement, confirmed: 'By default, the rollback uses the last release with a successful rollout to the indicated target, but you can choose a different one'
rewrite.statement: By default, a Cloud Deploy rollback redeploys the last release that had a successful rollout to that target.
rewrite.explanation: Cloud Deploy creates a new rollout from the last release that succeeded on the target unless the team picks another release; it does not rewind the earlier rollout.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (role names give the answer); verifier's replacement, reworded to avoid negation. Confirmed: 'By default, the IC assumes all roles that have not been delegated yet.'
rewrite.statement: In Google's incident response model, the Ops Lead takes on any incident role that remains undelegated.
rewrite.explanation: The SRE Workbook says the Incident Commander assumes every role not yet delegated, including Ops Lead; delegating them lets the IC focus on coordination and communication.
rewrite.misconception: The Ops Lead absorbs incident roles that nobody has been assigned.

rewrite.reason: tell: 'preserves' as the main verb marked false 4 of 4 times, and a 'Cloud Run' subject was 1 true to 4 false. Same fact and answer.
rewrite.statement: An app's session files in a Cloud Run instance's local filesystem carry over to its replacement instance.
rewrite.explanation: Cloud Run loses files in the instance's local writable filesystem when that instance stops. Session data needing persistence belongs in external storage.
rewrite.misconception: Cloud Run carries instance-local session files into replacement instances.

rewrite.reason: tell: 'preserves' marked false. Same fact and answer.
rewrite.statement: Datastream delivers change events into Cloud Storage in source commit order.
rewrite.explanation: Datastream delivers change events that can arrive out of order. A Cloud Storage consumer uses source-specific event metadata to reconstruct the source operation order.
rewrite.misconception: Datastream guarantees source commit order in the sequence of delivered change events.

rewrite.reason: tell: 'preserves' marked false. Same fact and answer.
rewrite.statement: The Bigtable emulator writes test data to local disk so a later emulator process can reuse it.
rewrite.explanation: The Bigtable emulator keeps its data in memory and loses it across runs. Tests that need an initial dataset populate that dataset for a new emulator run.
rewrite.misconception: The Bigtable emulator persists application data on local disk between processes.

rewrite.reason: tell: 'limits/confines ... to a single Z' marked false 4 of 4 times. Same fact and answer.
rewrite.statement: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus answers a PromQL query from a single Google Cloud region's data.
rewrite.explanation: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus evaluates queries against a global datastore and combines results across regions. Teams obtain a unified view rather than querying isolated regional servers.
rewrite.misconception: Managed Prometheus query evaluation is confined to one regional datastore.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus

cards.statement: Google's DR guide describes the cold pattern as one with spare recovery resources already in place before a disaster.
cards.explanation: In the cold pattern no spare resources are on hand, so recovery must first obtain them, and the service stays down until they arrive.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The fact lens quoted the planning guide's flat-tire analogy for cold (no spare tire).

cards.statement: DORA groups failed deployment recovery time with deployment frequency as a software delivery throughput factor.
cards.explanation: DORA measures throughput with change lead time, deployment frequency and failed deployment recovery time; change fail rate and deployment rework rate measure instability.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The dora.dev throughput and instability lists were confirmed. Volatility is may_change.

cards.statement: Compute flexible committed use discounts can reserve VM capacity for the committed workload.
cards.explanation: Compute flexible commitments don't support attached reservations and come with no assured capacity, so a workload that needs assured VM capacity uses a separate reservation.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The reservations-with-commitments page confirms there are no attached reservations and no assured capacity.

cards.statement: For a regional MIG spread across three zones, Google recommends overprovisioning the group by at least 50%.
cards.explanation: Losing one of three zones removes a third of capacity, so Google recommends at least 50% extra instances, and doubling for two zones, so the remaining zones carry the full load.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The regional MIGs page recommends at least 50% for three zones and +100% for two. The number is the fact that decides the design, so volatility is may_change.

cards.statement: Enabling Cloud CDN caching on a load balancer requires that load balancer to use Network Service Tiers' Premium Tier.
cards.explanation: Cloud CDN is always Premium Tier and can't be used with Standard Tier, so choosing Standard Tier to lower a load balancer's egress cost rules out Cloud CDN caching.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The Network Service Tiers overview says 'Cloud CDN is always Premium Tier' and 'You cannot use Standard Tier with Cloud CDN'.

cards.statement: A Project Owner can manually delete a backup vault's backups before their enforced retention ends.
cards.explanation: Enforced retention makes a vault's backups immutable: no user, including a Project Owner, and not even Google can manually delete them until the retention period has passed.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The backup vault page says nobody, Google included, can manually delete backups until the duration has passed. Lowering the minimum before the lock's effective date changes the retention, not deletion.

cards.statement: Each Shared VPC service project in an organization attaches to a single host project at any given time.
cards.explanation: A host project can share subnets with many service projects, but each service project can be attached to only one host project, so it uses that one host's Shared VPC network.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: the 'though one host can serve many' clause was a second fact and read as a true-statement tell. The fact lens confirmed 'each service project can only be attached to a single host project'. Same fact and answer, 103 characters.

cards.statement: By default, an external proxy Network Load Balancer passes client source IPs and ports through to its backends.
cards.explanation: By default the target proxy drops the original client IP and port, so backends see the proxy as the source. Enabling the PROXY protocol on the target proxy preserves that client information.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The load-balancing/docs/tcp page states the default and the PROXY protocol option.

cards.statement: One Migration Center TCO report can compare several migration preference sets for one asset group.
cards.explanation: When generating a TCO report, a team picks asset groups and assigns each group multiple preference sets, so one report compares migration scenarios side by side.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The generate-tco-report page lets a team assign up to four preference sets per group; the card leaves out the number.

cards.statement: Rehosting a workload on Google Cloud gives it horizontal scalability as part of the migration itself.
cards.explanation: Rehost moves workloads with minor or no changes, so Google notes they aren't optimized for the cloud afterwards and miss features such as horizontal scalability; replatform or refactor work adds that.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: 'run optimized for the cloud' was close to a definition card. The fix names horizontal scalability, a feature the getting-started page says rehosted workloads lack. Both lenses confirmed it. Same fact and answer.

cards.statement: Google classifies replacing on-premises collaboration software with Google Workspace as a repurchase migration.
cards.explanation: Repurchase means moving from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted SaaS equivalent, rather than moving its code or rebuilding it.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The getting-started page gives this Google Workspace example under repurchase.

cards.statement: BigQuery's pre-run cost estimate for a query on a clustered table can exceed the bytes the query finally scans.
cards.explanation: BigQuery learns which clustered blocks it can skip only during execution, so the estimate before a run isn't exact and the final cost reflects the blocks scanned. Partitioning gives granular pre-run estimates.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The clustered-tables page says BigQuery reduces bytes at execution, the final cost comes from the blocks scanned, and partitioning gives granular pre-run estimates.

cards.statement: A Spot VM keeps running until Compute Engine preempts it unless the team sets a limit on its run duration.
cards.explanation: Spot VMs have no minimum or maximum runtime unless you limit it, so a long batch job keeps running until preemption or until a run duration limit the team configured ends it.
cards.reason: Wording lens drop holds. I checked content/raw/gcp-ace-b1.json: gcp-ace-s2.1-03 ('Spot VMs can run for a maximum of 24 hours', false; 'Spot VMs have no fixed maximum runtime unless you configure one') already tests this fact, and the prompt forbids retesting an ACE fact. The lens suggested a replacement for a separate pass: Spot VMs in a MIG are repeatedly recreated after preemption.

cards.statement: A team running GKE Standard creates a separate Autopilot cluster to put some workloads on Autopilot-managed nodes.
cards.explanation: Autopilot ComputeClasses let a Standard cluster run selected workloads on Autopilot-managed node pools alongside the team's own Standard node pools, in the same cluster.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: the old wording ('Workloads a GKE Standard cluster puts on...') gave away that the workloads stay in the cluster. The fact lens confirmed same-cluster Autopilot-managed node pools on the page, which has no Preview label.

cards.statement: VMware Engine gives the default vCenter user full administrator access to vCenter in a private cloud.
cards.explanation: VMware Engine retains full administrative access to a private cloud; its default user, CloudOwner (at) gve.local, gets Cloud-Owner-Role privileges, enough to deploy and manage VMs.
cards.reason: Fact lens fix, checked: the Elevate page never names a default user. The permission model page (docs.cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/concepts-permission-model, updated 2026-10-07) says VMware Engine 'retains full administrative access' and that CloudOwner (at) gve.local gets Cloud-Owner-Role with 'sufficient administrator privileges' to deploy and manage VMs. Change the source to that page, titled 'Private cloud vSphere permission model'. That page's outdated elevation line is left out.

cards.statement: Cluster Director gives AI Hypercomputer GPU clusters a managed Slurm environment, so teams skip installing Slurm.
cards.explanation: For a managed Slurm experience Google points to Cluster Director, while Cluster Toolkit deploys blueprints that install Slurm on clusters the team runs itself.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The process-overview page points to Cluster Director for managed Slurm and to Cluster Toolkit for native Slurm, with no Preview label.

cards.statement: Gemini Enterprise uses project IAM grants to override source-document ACLs for ACL-enabled connectors.
cards.explanation: Gemini Enterprise uses your identity provider to check whether the end user can access each document a connector returns; IAM roles on the project grant no extra document access.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The configure-identity-provider page says Gemini Enterprise 'never bypasses source system access controls or grants additional permissions'.

cards.statement: When an administrator destroys a Cloud KMS key version, Cloud KMS erases its key material right away.
cards.explanation: Destroying a key version puts it in the scheduled-for-destruction state, 30 days by default and configurable at key creation, and it can be restored during that time.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: in the old statement 'schedules for destruction' gave away the delay. I checked kms/docs/destroy-restore: 'Key material isn't immediately destroyed', the default is 30 days, a custom duration is set at key creation, and the version can be restored. Volatility stays may_change.

cards.statement: Identity-Aware Proxy can apply Access Context Manager access levels, such as device or IP conditions, to app users.
cards.explanation: IAP attaches access levels to the IAM grants of an IAP-secured app, so users get in only from approved IP ranges or trusted devices; device attributes need a Chrome Enterprise Premium license.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The context-aware access how-to confirms IP and device access levels and the Chrome Enterprise Premium license.

cards.statement: Key Access Justifications lets a key policy deny a Cloud KMS request by its justification code.
cards.explanation: Beyond logging why a key is used, Key Access Justifications policies can approve or deny key access per justification code; this depends on the Assured Workloads control package chosen.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The KAJ overview confirms approve or deny by justification code for select control packages.

cards.statement: Infrastructure Manager previews cover first-time deployments as well as updates to existing deployments.
cards.explanation: An Infrastructure Manager preview runs Terraform plan for a new deployment or an update, so the team reviews the resources planned for provisioning before anything is created.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: the old statement was close to a definition of 'preview'. The fix tests that previews also cover new deployments, which the fact lens confirmed: 'Before you create a new deployment or update a deployment, you can preview the deployment'.

cards.statement: Google lists an on-call intervention, such as a release rollback, among the triggers for a postmortem.
cards.explanation: Google's postmortem criteria include on-call interventions such as a release rollback or rerouted traffic, alongside user-visible downtime, data loss of any kind and monitoring failures.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The conduct-postmortems page lists on-call interventions such as a release rollback; 'user-visible downtime' is acceptable shorthand for 'beyond a certain threshold'.

cards.statement: Google recommends restoring backups into production, where real dependencies run, when testing that they are usable.
cards.explanation: Google recommends restoring backups in a non-production environment and testing the entire application stack and critical infrastructure services with the restored data.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: it removes the strawman by giving the plausible reason someone might restore into production. The fact lens confirmed 'To test backups, restore them in a non-production environment'. Same fact and answer, 116 characters.

cards.statement: Google recommends granting users in the DR environment the access they hold in production.
cards.explanation: Users must be able to work in the recovered environment; when production runs on Google Cloud, IaC tools such as Terraform can replicate its IAM policies in the DR environment.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The DR planning guide says to grant users the same access in DR as in production and mentions replicating IAM policies with Terraform.

cards.statement: Cloud Billing exports show a new label's costs only from the date the label was applied to a resource.
cards.explanation: Labels aren't retroactive: the export shows a label's costs from the date it was applied, so apply labels before the period you need to allocate.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The detailed export page's labels note supports it, and 'only' matches the source.

cards.statement: Unused commitment from one hour of a standard spend-based CUD carries over to cover usage in a later hour.
cards.explanation: Standard spend-based CUDs apply hourly: if eligible usage in an hour falls below the commitment you still pay the full amount, and the unused part doesn't roll over. Flexible Savings Plans use a monthly window.
cards.reason: Fact lens fix holds. I checked cuds-multiprice: FSPs are 'a type of spend-based commitment' with a monthly entitlement window, while standard spend-based CUDs are hourly and 'Unused commitment does not carry over to the next hour'. The statement is now limited to standard spend-based CUDs.

cards.statement: Cloud Billing sizes its CUD recommendations from an organization's expected future usage growth.
cards.explanation: CUD recommendations come from historical and recent usage, including usage already covered by commitments, so architects weigh planned growth or decline themselves.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The cuds-recommender page says recommendations use historical and recent usage metrics.

cards.statement: GKE cost allocation must be enabled on a Standard cluster before billing exports show its namespace costs.
cards.explanation: Once GKE cost allocation is enabled, the detailed Cloud Billing export to BigQuery carries cluster, namespace and workload labels for chargeback; otherwise those costs carry no GKE labels.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The cost-allocations page says the export includes GKE labels from the date it is enabled, with no backfill, and only in the detailed export.

cards.statement: The Spanner emulator enforces IAM permissions on requests that an application's integration tests send to it.
cards.explanation: The Spanner emulator supports no authentication, IAM, permissions or roles, so access grants still need testing against a real Spanner instance.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The Spanner emulator page lists no authentication, IAM, permissions or roles. With s5.2-06 it is the second and last allowed emulator false card.

cards.statement: Infrastructure Manager keeps a Terraform state file per deployment and per revision.
cards.explanation: Infrastructure Manager creates a Terraform state file per deployment and per revision; a team can download a state file to inspect or modify it.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The state-file page confirms a Terraform state file for each deployment and revision.

cards.statement: To export logs received before a sink existed, Cloud Logging offers a copy from the log bucket to Cloud Storage.
cards.explanation: Sinks route only entries that arrive after they're created; for entries already stored in a log bucket, Cloud Logging can copy them retroactively to Cloud Storage.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The routing overview says sinks can't route retroactively but log data can be copied retroactively to Cloud Storage.

cards.statement: Cloud Profiler can collect profiles from applications that run outside Google Cloud, such as on premises.
cards.explanation: Cloud Profiler agents for Go, Java, Node.js and Python also run outside Google Cloud, so hybrid workloads can send low-overhead profiles to a Google Cloud project; profile types vary by language.
cards.reason: Fact lens fix, checked on about-profiler: 'Outside of Google Cloud' is Y for all four languages, but CPU time and Heap are not marked for every language, so 'CPU and heap profiles' is replaced by 'profile types vary by language'. The statement is unchanged.

cards.statement: Setting maxUnavailable to 0 in a MIG rolling update removes the need for spare quota during the update.
cards.explanation: With maxUnavailable at 0 and maxSurge above 0, the MIG creates each replacement VM before deleting the old one, and maxSurge only works when there is quota and capacity for the extra VMs.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The rolling-updates page confirms surge-before-delete and that maxSurge needs quota. The edge case of both values at 0 forces maxUnavailable to 1, so the answer holds.

cards.statement: By default, a Cloud Deploy rollback redeploys the last release that had a successful rollout to that target.
cards.explanation: Cloud Deploy creates a new rollout from the last release that succeeded on the target unless the team picks another release; it does not rewind the earlier rollout.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The Cloud Deploy roll-back page confirms the default and the new rollout resource.

cards.statement: In Google's incident response model, the Ops Lead takes on any incident role that remains undelegated.
cards.explanation: The SRE Workbook says the Incident Commander assumes every role not yet delegated, including Ops Lead; delegating them lets the IC focus on coordination and communication.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The SRE Workbook says 'By default, the IC assumes all roles that have not been delegated yet.'

cards.statement: An app's session files in a Cloud Run instance's local filesystem carry over to its replacement instance.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run loses files in the instance's local writable filesystem when that instance stops. Session data needing persistence belongs in external storage.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The container contract says written files don't persist when the instance stops.

cards.statement: Datastream delivers change events into Cloud Storage in source commit order.
cards.explanation: Datastream delivers change events that can arrive out of order. A Cloud Storage consumer uses source-specific event metadata to reconstruct the source operation order.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The events-and-streams page says 'Datastream doesn't guarantee ordering' and that ordering is inferred per source.

cards.statement: The Bigtable emulator writes test data to local disk so a later emulator process can reuse it.
cards.explanation: The Bigtable emulator keeps its data in memory and loses it across runs. Tests that need an initial dataset populate that dataset for a new emulator run.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The Bigtable emulator page says it stores data only in memory and won't persist it across runs.

cards.statement: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus answers a PromQL query from a single Google Cloud region's data.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus evaluates queries against a global datastore and combines results across regions. Teams obtain a unified view rather than querying isolated regional servers.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The managed-prometheus page says Monarch unions query results across all Google Cloud regions.

cards.statement: Compute Engine's default sole-tenant maintenance policy live-migrates VMs within a fixed server pool.
cards.explanation: Compute Engine's Default sole-tenant maintenance policy lets eligible VMs migrate to new physical servers. Migrate within node group confines migration to a fixed server pool.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. The sole-tenant page contrasts the Default policy with Migrate within node group.
